CONCLUSION: Digital strategies appear to improve GDMT optimization in HFrEF, particularly when embedded within structured care pathways that enable repeated reassessment and protocol-driven titration. Passive alerts alone appear less effective. Standardized outcome measures and trials evaluating clinical endpoints are needed.

Title: Prognostic impact of long-term beta-blockers post-stemi: a meta-analytic review.
Abstract:
AIMS: This meta-analysis assessed the long-term impact of beta-blocker therapy on all-cause mortality and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) who continued beta-blocker use for a minimum of 1 year after hospital discharge.
METHODS: Electronic databases were searched through September 2024 to identify studies comparing long-term outcomes in patients treated with beta-blockers versus those untreated. A random-effects model was used to estimate Hazard Ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
RESULTS: A total of 21 studies involving 270 566 patients were included. In pooled analyses, extended beta-blocker was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality in STEMI patients [HR: 0.74 (0.66, 0.83); P < 0.0001] and showing non-significant trend toward reducing cardiac death [HR: 0.77 (0.56, 1.04); P = 0.09], an effect observed predominantly in observational studies. However, in randomized controlled trials (N = 3), no significant benefit was demonstrated (all-cause mortality: P = 0.67; cardiac death: P = 0.62). No meaningful differences were found for major adverse cardiovascular events [HR: 0.90 (0.76, 1.07); P = 0.22], myocardial infarction, hospitalization for heart failure, or revascularization.
CONCLUSION: Long-term beta-blocker use is associated with a significant reduction in all-cause mortality among STEMI patients, though this benefit was not seen in RCTs. Effects on other cardiovascular outcomes remain uncertain, highlighting the need for further large-scale trials.

Title: Overcoming Hyperkalaemia to Optimise Heart Failure Therapy: The Emerging Role of Novel Potassium Binders.
Abstract: Hyperkalaemia is common in patients with heart failure. It limits the initiation, optimisation and continuation of guideline-directed medical therapy, particularly mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists. Two potassium binders, patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC), have emerged as strategies to address this barrier. SZC is an inorganic crystalline compound that binds potassium in exchange for sodium and hydrogen throughout the gastrointestinal tract, resulting in rapid potassium lowering, whereas patiromer is a non-absorbed organic polymer that exchanges potassium for calcium in the colon and has a slower onset of action. Both agents have demonstrated efficacy in maintaining normokalaemia and enabling the continuation of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitor therapy in heart failure. Differences in electrolyte effects and tolerability have clinical implications: patiromer is associated with hypomagnesaemia, while SZC delivers a sodium load that may predispose patients to fluid retention. However, no head-to-head randomised trials are available and evidence for improvement in heart failure morbidity or mortality remains limited, underscoring the need for adequately powered outcome studies.

Title: Restrictive vs. liberal blood transfusion strategies in Africa: clinical outcomes, resource stewardship, and future directions.
Abstract: Blood transfusion continues to be a vital part of contemporary healthcare, especially in treating severe anemia, bleeding, trauma, obstetric crises, and critical conditions. In Africa, where transfusion-dependent conditions are prevalent and blood supplies often limited, establishing the best transfusion threshold is crucial for enhancing patient outcomes while maximizing the use of scarce resources. Restrictive transfusion practices that typically use lower hemoglobin thresholds (7-8 g/dL) are now widely accepted globally as they minimize unnecessary transfusions while maintaining safety across various clinical environments. In contrast, liberal approaches, defined by elevated transfusion thresholds (9-10 g/dL), might still be suitable for specific patient groups, such as individuals with acute coronary syndromes, persistent significant bleeding, or serious symptomatic anemia. This review analyzes the existing evidence regarding restrictive vs. liberal blood transfusion strategies in the African context, focusing on clinical outcomes, resource management in healthcare, and prospective avenues for practice and investigation. Research from randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and global guidelines consistently shows that restrictive transfusion strategies correlate with similar mortality, morbidity, hospital stay duration, and functional recovery in most stable hospitalized patients, while minimizing transfusion-related complications and preserving limited blood resources. Nevertheless, the direct relevance of evidence produced mainly in high-income countries needs thorough evaluation due to Africa's distinct epidemiological characteristics, healthcare system constraints, and blood service deficiencies. Enhancing patient blood management initiatives, increasing voluntary blood donations, improving transfusion oversight, and producing robust African clinical evidence are essential priorities.

Title: Applications of artificial intelligence in personalized nutrition interventions.
Abstract: Unhealthy dietary patterns remain a major modifiable contributor to the global burden of obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), cardiovascular disease, and cancer. However, individuals can respond markedly differently to identical foods, limiting the effectiveness of one-size-fits-all dietary guidance. This review examines the application of artificial intelligence (AI) to personalized nutrition interventions across three interconnected layers. At the biological level, inter-individual variability can be characterized by three mechanistic dimensions: nutrigenomic variation, which influences nutrient metabolism and disease susceptibility; metabolomic biomarkers, which objectively capture dietary exposure and early metabolic alterations; and the gut microbiome, which bidirectionally mediates diet-host interactions. At the technological level, AI integrates these dimensions into multimodal digital profiles. Machine learning models predict individual postprandial glycemic and lipemic responses, with reported correlations of up to r = 0.77 in large cohorts; deep learning and computer vision automate dietary assessment; natural language processing and large language models (LLMs) support nutrition counseling; knowledge graphs enable constraint-aware food recommendations; and digital-twin and adaptive closed-loop systems incorporating continuous glucose monitoring and wearable-device data support real-time nutritional interventions. However, the strength of clinical evidence varies across disease domains. Glycemic management in T2DM and prediabetes currently has the most mature randomized controlled trial evidence: an AI-enabled personalized intervention combining algorithmic dietary personalization with CGM-linked feedback improved glycemic endpoints compared with a Mediterranean diet, while a fully automated AI-delivered diabetes prevention program achieved outcomes non-inferior to those of human coaching. In obesity, cardiovascular disease, oncology, and gastrointestinal disorders, the evidence remains mixed or preliminary. Clinical translation also faces substantial challenges, including biased and inconsistently standardized dietary and multi-omics data; the underrepresentation of non-European populations, which limits model generalizability and raises concerns about health equity; limited model explainability; privacy and data-governance challenges; immature regulatory pathways for adaptive software as a medical device; and specific risks associated with LLMs, such as hallucinated or guideline-discordant dietary advice. AI-enabled personalized nutrition is therefore progressing from proof of concept toward clinical translation. Realizing its potential equitably will require multi-ethnic nutrition-omics cohorts, privacy-preserving multicenter collaboration, dietitian-led human-AI collaboration, and lifecycle safety governance for generative models.

Title: Short-term clinical outcomes of nasoduodenal tube versus feeding jejunostomy after minimally invasive esophagectomy: a retrospective cohort study with exploratory microbiome analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Esophagectomy remains an effective treatment for esophageal cancer but is associated with severe postoperative complications, in which nutritional status plays a critical role. The optimal route for enteral feeding remains uncertain. To address this uncertainty, we compared the short-term clinical outcomes of the two approaches and exploratorily analyzed the differences in gut microbiota.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study enrolled patients who underwent minimally invasive esophagectomy (MIE) for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) between July 2018 and June 2021. Primary outcomes were surgery-related complications (including anastomotic leakage, anastomotic stenosis, pneumonia, respiratory failure, cardiac events, chylothorax, intestinal fistula and bowel obstruction) and catheter-related outcomes (including occlusion, accidental removal, displacement and retention time). Baseline data were extracted from medical records. Propensity score matching (PSM) was applied to control for potential confounders. Intestinal fluid and fecal samples were collected after enteral nutrition for 16S ribosomal DNA (16S rDNA) sequencing.
RESULTS: After PSM, a total of 381 patients (nasoduodenal tube: 282; feeding jejunostomy: 153) was finally included. The feeding jejunostomy group exhibited a higher incidence of pneumonia (21.49% vs. 33.99%, P=0.007), respiratory failure (3.07% vs. 13.07%, P<0.001), anastomotic stenosis (1.32% vs. 5.23%, P=0.03) and bowel obstruction (0% vs. 2.16%, P=0.03). Nasoduodenal tube placement was associated with more accidental removal (13.16% vs. 0.65%, P<0.001) and catheter displacement (13.60% vs. 6.54%, P=0.03). The catheter retention time {37 [interquartile range (IQR): 15-40] days vs. 39 (IQR: 37-42) days, P<0.001} was also shorter in nasoduodenal tube group.
CONCLUSIONS: In this study, nasoduodenal tube placement was associated with a higher incidence of catheter-related complications, whereas feeding jejunostomy was linked to more surgery-related complications. Nasoduodenal tube placement also showed potential functional advantages for the gut microbiome. However, future multi-center randomized controlled trials are still needed to minimize potential confounders and validate the differences between the two enteral nutrition routes.

Title: Liposomal bupivacaine versus ropivacaine thoracic paravertebral block for thoracoscopic atrial septal defect repair: analgesic efficacy and cardiac biomarker outcomes in a single-center, assessor-blinded, randomized trial.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thoracoscopic atrial septal defect (ASD) repair, although minimally invasive, can cause substantial postoperative pain. Thoracic paravertebral block (TPVB) provides effective chest wall analgesia, and liposomal bupivacaine (LB), a long-acting local anesthetic with sustained release, may prolong analgesic duration. We investigated whether ultrasound-guided TPVB using long-acting LB improves postoperative analgesia without compromising cardiovascular safety compared with ropivacaine (RP).
METHODS: This randomized, assessor-blinded trial enrolled 94 patients undergoing thoracoscopic ASD repair, who were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive ultrasound-guided TPVB with either LB or RP. Eligibility criteria included age 18-55 years, American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) II-III, New York Heart Association (NYHA) II-III, and ejection fraction (EF) >50%. Randomization was computer-generated with sealed envelopes. Safety monitoring included continuous electrocardiography (ECG) for arrhythmias, with Clavien-Dindo grading and Naranjo causality assessment. The primary endpoint was the numerical rating scale (NRS, 0-10) pain score during coughing at 24 h postoperatively. Secondary outcomes included NRS scores at other time points, 72-h opioid consumption (morphine milligram equivalents, MME), time to first rescue analgesia, extended analgesia outcomes [postoperative days 4-7 (POD4-POD7)], perioperative hemodynamics, postoperative recovery, cardiac/inflammatory biomarker trajectories, and adverse events (with postoperative arrhythmias analyzed separately).
RESULTS: Baseline demographic, clinical, and intraoperative variables were well-balanced between groups (all P>0.05). Compared with RP, LB was associated with lower NRS pain scores at rest and during coughing from extubation through 72 h (all P<0.05), including the primary endpoint at 24 h. LB significantly reduced 72-h opioid consumption [median interquartile range (IQR) 7.5 (0, 42) mg vs. 45 (30, 67.5) mg; P<0.001] and increased the proportion of patients requiring no rescue analgesia within 72 h (72.4% vs. 27.6%; P=0.003). Time to first rescue analgesia was numerically longer with LB (20.5 h vs. 12.0 h; P=0.10), and opioid-sparing effects persisted on POD4-POD7 (both P<0.001). Mechanical ventilation duration was shorter in the LB group [5 (3, 6) h vs. 6 (4, 7.5) h; P=0.03]. Cardiac and inflammatory biomarker trajectories did not differ between groups. Non-arrhythmic adverse events were comparable, and postoperative arrhythmia incidence within 30 days was similar between groups (13.3% vs. 15.6%).
CONCLUSIONS: In adults undergoing thoracoscopic ASD repair, LB-based TPVB provides superior early analgesia with sustained opioid sparing and shorter mechanical ventilation duration, without signals of increased cardiovascular risk, including postoperative arrhythmias. These findings support considering LB-TPVB as part of multimodal analgesia for thoracoscopic ASD repair, pending confirmation in larger multicenter studies.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ChiCTR2500112278, retrospectively registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry on November 12, 2025.

Title: Comparative efficacy of digital health intervention delivery modalities on quality of life, anxiety, and depression in coronary heart disease: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Nonadherence to traditional cardiac rehabilitation and persistent psychological distress among patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) severely undermine desired therapeutic outcomes. Digital health interventions (DHIs) emerge as promising strategies to effectively tackle this adherence and mental health issue remotely.
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to conduct a network meta-analysis (NMA) to compare and rank the comparative efficacy of various DHI delivery modalities in improving quality of life (QoL), anxiety, and depression among patients with CHD.
METHODS: A systematic search strategy was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane, CNKI, VIP, WanFang, and SinoMed databases to search for randomized controlled trials (RCTs)published from their inception to February 1,2026.We carried out a frequentist NMA using Stata 18.0to compare the efficacy of various DHIs against standard care. The quality of literature was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (version2.0).The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework, and interventions were ranked utilizing the surface under the cumulative ranking (SUCRA)curve.
RESULTS: A total of 44RCTs involving 8,495 patients were enrolled. The NMA revealed that for improving QoL, telephone follow-up (standardized mean difference 2.98, 95%CI 1.75-4.20) and social media (SMD 1.13, 95%CI 0.42-1.84) were statistically superior to usual care. Notably, telephone follow-up, with a SUCRA of 99.5%, appeared to be the most effective option. Regarding psychological outcomes, web-based platforms demonstrated the highest probability of being the best intervention for reducing both anxiety (SMD -1.56,95%CI-2.34 to -0.79;SUCRA 98.6%) and depression (SMD-1.07,95%CI-1.94to-0.20;SUCRA 91.4%).Safety analyses showed interactive modalities significantly reduced adverse events, whereas one-way SMS carried a significantly higher risk than interactive telephone support(OR 3.38,95%CI 1.13-10.13).
CONCLUSIONS: The research suggests that telephone follow-up ranked highest among the included studies for improving short-term QoL, while web-based platforms showed a high probability of being effective for alleviating long-term anxiety and depression. However, these rankings should be interpreted cautiously, as intervention content, duration, and patient populations varied considerably across trials, and the small number of studies for certain modalities limits the robustness of direct comparisons. Social media interventions also emerged as a versatile option with benefits across all three outcomes, though their modest effect sizes warrant further optimization of engagement strategies. Passive SMS interventions present potential safety concerns, as their unidirectional nature may attenuate timely symptom recognition and delay appropriate care-seeking-a hypothesis supported by their significantly higher adverse event rates compared with interactive modalities. These results provide crucial evidence-based support for healthcare providers to tailor specific DHIs to individual patient needs.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420261380157.

Title: Vascular access options for complex high-risk indicated percutaneous coronary interventions: contemporary strategies, trade-offs, and practical algorithms.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Vascular access is an important component of CHIP planning that influences procedural feasibility, safety, and completeness. It affects bleeding and vascular complications, guide-catheter support, compatibility with intravascular imaging and calcium-modification devices, chronic total occlusion techniques, closure and bailout options, and mechanical circulatory support (MCS) planning. Contemporary CHIP populations are increasingly older or frail and more often have chronic kidney disease, peripheral artery disease, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, prior bypass surgery, calcification, or CTO; access choice should extend beyond radial vs. femoral.
SUMMARY: This review appraises proximal and distal radial, femoral, ulnar, and brachial access; sheathless, slender, and RailTracking strategies; large-bore femoral workflows; and access planning when MCS is considered. We discuss preprocedural arterial assessment, ultrasound and micropuncture, prior access footprint, closure feasibility, hostile femoral anatomy, alternative access, and complication prevention and rescue. The available literature supports a non-dogmatic approach in which access architecture is matched to patient vulnerability, arterial anatomy, lesion complexity, guide and device requirements, support needs, haemostasis feasibility, and bailout planning. Recent randomised evidence further reinforces selective rather than routine prophylactic MCS in nonemergent high-risk PCI.
CONCLUSIONS: Forearm access should remain central whenever it permits procedural success without compromising device delivery, imaging, guide support, or bailout flexibility. Femoral access remains indispensable when large-bore support, maximal guide stability, complex device delivery, or rapid escalation are anticipated. Within a comprehensive CHIP plan, the preferred access architecture is the smallest one that enables the intended revascularisation, safe haemostasis, and timely rescue.

Title: Residual atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk in statin-treated patients: mechanisms, therapeutic strategies, and future directions-a scoping review.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Statins remain the cornerstone of pharmacological prevention for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) because of their proven ability to reduce low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). However, many patients continue to experience ASCVD events despite achieving guideline-recommended LDL-C targets with maximally tolerated statin therapy, highlighting the persistence of residual ASCVD risk. This scoping review synthesized current evidence on residual ASCVD risk in statin-treated patients, focusing on its epidemiology, underlying mechanisms, clinical evidence, therapeutic strategies beyond statins, and barriers to optimal risk reduction.
METHODS: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. Electronic databases were systematically searched, yielding 1,240 records. After duplicate removal and screening, 195 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 35 studies were included in the final qualitative synthesis. The included evidence comprised randomized controlled trials, observational cohort studies, registry-based investigations, and systematic and narrative reviews.
RESULTS: The included studies were synthesized into five major themes: epidemiology of residual ASCVD risk, underlying mechanisms, clinical evidence from landmark trials and real-world studies, therapeutic strategies beyond statins, and challenges limiting effective risk reduction. Evidence consistently demonstrated that residual ASCVD risk persists despite substantial LDL-C reduction because of multiple interacting factors, including elevated triglyceride-rich remnant lipoproteins, lipoprotein(a), persistent inflammation, metabolic comorbidities, vascular aging, treatment-implementation barriers, and behavioral factors. Landmark clinical trials, including IMPROVE-IT, FOURIER, ODYSSEY OUTCOMES, REDUCE-IT, CANTOS, LoDoCo2, and CLEAR Outcomes, demonstrated incremental cardiovascular benefit from combination lipid-lowering and selected anti-inflammatory therapies, while emerging therapies targeting lipoprotein(a), IL-6 signaling, and RNA-based pathways offer promising strategies for further reducing residual ASCVD risk.
CONCLUSION: Residual ASCVD risk remains a major challenge despite guideline-directed statin therapy. Effective risk reduction requires a comprehensive approach that extends beyond LDL-C lowering to include combination lipid-lowering therapy, inflammation-targeted interventions, lifestyle optimization, improved treatment adherence, and individualized risk assessment. Continued evaluation of emerging therapies and precision medicine approaches is essential to further reduce the global burden of ASCVD.

Title: Comparative efficacy of Traditional Chinese Medicine classical prescriptions for angina pectoris: a network meta-analysis.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of classical prescriptions from Shang han Lun (Treatise on Febrile Diseases) and Jin gui Yao lue (Synopsis of the Golden Chamber) combined with conventional biomedicine in the treatment of angina pectoris of coronary heart disease.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Eight commonly used Chinese and English databases were searched for relevant clinical studies published before 25 December 2024. Revman 5.4 and Stata14.0 software were used for data analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 131 studies involving 11,292 participants (5,660 in intervention groups and 5,632 in control groups) were included. Most classical prescriptions combined with conventional biomedical therapy showed favorable associations with improvements in angina pectoris efficiency, electrocardiogram (ECG) efficiency, and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) syndrome outcomes compared with conventional treatment alone. Subgroup analyses showed partially different patterns of relative efficacy among prescriptions, with LGZG demonstrating more consistent performance in stable angina pectoris, while other prescriptions showed variable rankings in unstable angina pectoris. For lipid-related and inflammatory outcomes, results were inconsistent across studies, and current evidence remains insufficient to support robust comparative conclusions among classical prescriptions. Regarding safety outcomes, GZFL combined with conventional biomedical therapy showed a relatively favorable safety profile, while other classical prescriptions demonstrated comparable rates of adverse events to conventional therapy.
CONCLUSION: Classical prescriptions combined with conventional biomedical therapy may be associated with improvements in clinical outcomes of angina pectoris, with an overall acceptable safety profile observed across most intervention. However, due to limitations in study quality, heterogeneity, and indirect comparisons, these findings should be interpreted with caution. Further high-quality, multicenter randomized controlled trials are required to confirm these observations.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251029216.

Title: SGLT2 Inhibitors Reduce Heart Failure Hospitalization, Cardiovascular Death and Kidney Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease are the principal drivers of morbidity and mortality in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have demonstrated cardiorenal benefits in landmark trials, yet cross-trial inconsistencies in cardiovascular mortality, renal endpoints and drug-specific effects leave the class-level estimates incompletely synthesized.
METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus and CENTRAL were searched from inception through 15 May 2026. Large placebo-controlled RCTs (≥ 1000 participants) and prespecified subgroup analyses in adults with T2DM were eligible. The primary outcome was the composite of first hospitalization for heart failure (HHF) or cardiovascular death (CV death). Secondary outcomes were 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), CV DEATH, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, first HHF and composite kidney outcomes. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using random-effects inverse-variance models.
RESULTS: Fourteen studies (76 969 patients; 41 761 SGLT2i, 35 208 placebo) were included. SGLT2i reduced the primary composite by 23% (HR: 0.77, 95% CI: 0.73-0.81, p < 0.0001; I2 = 0%), with no effect modification by baseline HF (p-interaction = 0.82) or established ASCVD (p-interaction = 0.46). MACE was reduced by 14% (HR: 0.86, 95% CI: 0.81-0.92), driven by significant reductions in CV DEATH (HR: 0.86, 95% CI: 0.79-0.93) and MI (HR: 0.88, 95% CI: 0.81-0.96), with no significant effect on stroke (HR: 0.93, 95% CI: 0.81-1.08). First, HHF was reduced by 29% (HR: 0.71, 95% CI: 0.66-0.77) and composite kidney outcomes by 31% (HR: 0.69, 95% CI: 0.60-0.79).
CONCLUSIONS: SGLT2i confer consistent and clinically meaningful cardiorenal protection in T2DM across the full spectrum of cardiovascular and renal risk. The ertugliflozin estimate and the moderate heterogeneity in kidney outcomes should be interpreted in the context of trial-level clinical differences and nonstandardized kidney endpoint definitions. These findings support proactive, guideline-concordant initiation of evidence-based SGLT2i agents by endocrinologists, cardiologists and primary care providers as foundational therapy in T2DM.

Title: Intelligent thermoregulation strategy versus routine thermal management on myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery during gastrointestinal tumor resection in elderly patients (SAGE): a multicenter, parallel-group, superiority trial.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Inadvertent perioperative hypothermia is associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes, but adequately powered trials using high-sensitivity troponin endpoints is lacking. The SAGE trial evaluates whether an intelligent, closed-loop thermoregulation strategy reduces myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery (MINS) in high-risk elderly patients.
METHODS: This prospective, multicenter, parallel-group, randomized controlled superiority trial conducted at seven tertiary hospitals in China. Participants aged ≥65 years scheduled for elective gastrointestinal tumor resection under general anesthesia are randomly assigned (1:1) to intelligent closed-loop warming (target 36.8 °C, upper limit 37.0 °C) or routine thermal management (active warming only if core temperature ≤35.5 °C). The primary outcome is the incidence of MINS within the first 2 postoperative days , adjudicated using high-sensitivity troponin thresholds per AHA criteria. Secondary outcomes include surgical site infection, transfusion requirement, hypothermia burden, emergence delirium, delayed emergence, and postoperative shivering. With 695 participants per group (total 1,390, accounting for 10% dropout), the trial has 80% power at a one-sided significance level of 0.05 to detect a 6 absolute percentage point reduction in MINS (12% to 6%) with a superiority margin of -2 percentage points.
DISCUSSION: The SAGE trial is designed to generate new evidence on the relationship between intraoperative hypothermia exposure and postoperative cardiovascular complications. It will evaluate whether closed-loop targeted normothermia reduces myocardial injury and will explore hypothermia exposure thresholds that may inform individualized perioperative management for geriatric surgical patients.
TRIAL ACRONYM: Intelligent Thermoregulation Strategy for Advanced-Age Elders undergoing gastrointestinal tumor resection (SAGE).
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR), identifier: ChiCTR2600117264. Registered on January 21, 2026 (http://www.chictr.org.cn).

Title: Medication-induced Micronutrient Deficiencies in Early-stage Chronic Kidney Disease.
Journal: Recent advances in food, nutrition & agriculture
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a growing global health burden, with early-stage patients often managed through long-term pharmacotherapy. However, prolonged use of common medications may unintentionally disrupt micronutrient balance, compounding the metabolic and cardiovascular risks already present in CKD.
OBJECTIVE: This narrative review aims to explore the associations between frequently prescribed medications and the development of micronutrient deficiencies in early-stage, non-dialysis CKD patients, highlighting underlying mechanisms, clinical implications, and potential management strategies.
METHODS: Relevant literature published between 2020 and 2025 was identified through structured searches of PubMed, MEDLINE, and the Cochrane Library. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials, observational cohorts, and prior reviews evaluating the effects of medications on micronutrient status in CKD stages 1-3. Evidence was narratively synthesized according to medication class, nutrient affected, and reported clinical outcomes.
RESULTS: Approximately 30-35 key studies were included. Phosphate binders, diuretics, antihypertensives, proton pump inhibitors, and immunosuppressants were most commonly associated with disruptions in vitamin D, iron, vitamin B12, calcium, and magnesium metabolism. These imbalances may contribute to anemia, mineral bone disorder, cardiovascular complications, and immune dysfunction in early CKD.
DISCUSSION: These findings suggest that medication-induced micronutrient disturbances may act as modifiable contributors to anemia, mineral-bone disorder, cardiovascular risk, and immune dysfunction in early-stage CKD. Routine nutritional monitoring alongside pharmacotherapy may therefore represent an important preventive strategy.
CONCLUSION: Medication-induced micronutrient deficiencies represent a clinically relevant yet underrecognized challenge in CKD management. The findings of this review are hypothesisgenerating and underscore the need for systematic, longitudinal research to establish causal pathways and inform evidence-based supplementation guidelines. Integrating nutritional monitoring into pharmacologic care may improve outcomes in early-stage CKD.

Title: Cannabinoids for Acute Pain Management: A Contemporary Scoping Review of Evidence, Mechanisms, and Clinical Implications.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The global opioid crisis has intensified interest in non-opioid and opioid-sparing analgesic strategies, including cannabinoids. Despite the expanding legal landscape for cannabis and a rapidly growing cannabinoid market, the clinical evidence for cannabinoid use in acute pain management remains inconsistent and largely of low quality.
METHODS: This contemporary scoping review was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A systematic search of six electronic databases (Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed/MEDLINE, ClinicalKey, EMBASE, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), and BIOSIS) was performed for literature published between 1 January 2016 and 5 April 2026, with the final database search executed on 5 April 2026, addressing the pharmacology, mechanisms of action, clinical efficacy, safety, and perioperative implications of cannabinoids in acute and postoperative pain. Two blinded reviewers independently screened records and charted data against predefined eligibility criteria; discrepancies were resolved by a third author. Findings are summarized narratively and in tabular format, and the study selection process is depicted in a PRISMA flow diagram.
RESULTS: Preclinical evidence supports robust antinociceptive effects of cannabinoids through multiple receptor pathways; however, these findings have not translated reliably into human acute pain models. Metaanalytic data demonstrate either no significant reduction in acute pain scores with cannabinoids versus placebo, or only small, clinically uncertain improvements. The opioid-sparing effect, while promising in preclinical and some chronic pain studies, has not been demonstrated for acute postoperative pain. A notable exception is a 2024 randomized trial showing a 40% reduction in opioid requirements with perioperative dronabinol after cardiac surgery. Safety data indicate that non-serious adverse events (dizziness, nausea, sedation) are consistently more frequent with cannabinoids than placebo. The 2023 American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine (ASRA) consensus guidelines now formalize 21 recommendations for perioperative cannabinoid management.
CONCLUSION: While the biological rationale for cannabinoid analgesia is compelling, the clinical evidence base for acute pain remains insufficient to support routine use. Cannabinoids may serve as adjuncts in specific populations, but require careful patient selection, dose titration, and safety monitoring. Well-designed, large randomized controlled trials targeting defined acute pain populations are urgently needed.

Title: Nurse Practitioner-Led Integration of Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Patients With Obesity-Related Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Prospective Clinical Effectiveness Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is characterized by systemic inflammation and reduced functional capacity. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) improve symptoms and weight in randomized trials, but uptake in routine cardiovascular practice is inconsistent.
OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this study was to evaluate a structured nurse practitioner-led program for GLP-1 RA initiation in obesity-related HFpEF.
METHODS: Prospective 12-month, single-center pre-post effectiveness study at a U.S. urban academic outpatient cardiology clinic. Adults with left ventricular ejection fraction ≥45%, body mass index ≥30 kg/m2, New York Heart Association class II-III symptoms, and at least 1 cardiometabolic comorbidity were enrolled. The intervention included registry-based identification, baseline assessment, patient education, protocolized titration, and longitudinal follow-up. Each participant's 12-month preenrollment period served as a comparator. The primary outcome was GLP-1 RA initiation and 12-month persistence.
RESULTS: Of 156 enrolled, 128 (82.1%) completed follow-up. Mean age 67.4 ± 11.2 years; 61.7% female; 43.8% Black. GLP-1 RA use rose from 7.8% to 92.2% (87.5% at target dose). Mean weight decreased 6.2 ± 3.8 kg, Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score improved 16.6 ± 11.3 points, and 6-minute walk distance rose 48.3 ± 36.2 m (all P < .001). Systolic blood pressure, hemoglobin A1c (diabetic subgroup), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide all decreased significantly. Heart failure hospitalization fell from 18.2% to 4.7% (P = .002). Gastrointestinal symptoms were most common; 4.7% discontinued for intolerance.
CONCLUSIONS: A structured nurse practitioner-led cardiometabolic program was associated with high GLP-1 RA initiation and persistence and with clinically meaningful improvements in symptoms, function, and hospitalization in obesity-related HFpEF.

Title: Robotic-assisted versus conventional coronary artery bypass grafting: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis of 39,918 patients.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Robotic-assisted coronary artery bypass grafting (RA-CABG) is an evolving minimally invasive alternative to conventional CABG (C-CABG), but comparative evidence remains fragmented. We conducted a comprehensive systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis to compare outcomes between RA-CABG and C-CABG.
METHODS: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science through January 2026. Studies comparing RA-CABG to C-CABG reporting at least one outcome of interest were eligible. Random-effects meta-analyses using DerSimonian-Laird estimators were performed. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I. Trial sequential analysis evaluated the conclusiveness of cumulative evidence.
RESULTS: Nine studies comprising 39,918 patients (13,638 RA-CABG; 26,280 C-CABG) were included. All included studies were observational in design, and long-term outcome data were sparse. RA-CABG was associated with significantly lower mortality (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.43-0.69; P < 0.001; I²=0%), atrial fibrillation (OR 0.53; P < 0.001), respiratory failure (OR 0.31; P < 0.001), blood transfusion (OR 0.28; P < 0.001), hospital length of stay (MD - 1.95 days; P < 0.001), and ICU stay (MD - 22.7 h; P < 0.001). Stroke showed a non-significant trend favoring RA-CABG (OR 0.76; P = 0.071). Trial sequential analysis confirmed conclusive evidence for mortality, atrial fibrillation, respiratory failure, and blood transfusion. Results were robust across sensitivity analyses.
CONCLUSIONS: In this meta-analysis of observational studies, RA-CABG was associated with significantly improved short-term outcomes compared to C-CABG across multiple endpoints, with conclusive statistical evidence for four of seven binary outcomes. However, all included studies were observational, and these associations should be interpreted with caution given potential residual confounding and case-selection bias. Multicenter randomized trials with long-term follow-up are needed to confirm these findings.

Title: Comparative effectiveness of dietary supplements in dilated cardiomyopathy: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a major cause of heart failure and cardiovascular mortality, partly due to impaired myocardial energy metabolism. Dietary supplements may offer benefits through improved mitochondrial function and antioxidant effects, and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) suggest they can enhance cardiac function in DCM. However, direct comparisons among supplements are lacking, and the optimal strategy and dose-response relationship remain undetermined.
METHODS: Eight databases were searched for RCTs evaluating dietary supplements in DCM. Continuous outcomes were analysed by frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis (NMA; Stata/MP 18.0); N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and New York Heart Association (NYHA) class were synthesised by pairwise meta-analysis. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool and certainty of evidence with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach.
RESULTS: Fourteen RCTs (1,259 participants) were included. For left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) 150 mg/d produced the largest improvement versus conventional treatment (CT) (mean difference [MD] = 11.26, 95% confidence interval [CI] 8.55 ~ 13.98; surface under the cumulative ranking curve [SUCRA] 93.4%), followed by taurine and CoQ10 90 mg/d. CoQ10 150 mg/d also ranked first for reducing left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (LVEDD; -5.40, - 8.14 ~ - 2.66) and end-systolic diameter (LVESD; -6.31, - 8.60 ~ - 4.01). For heart rate, n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFAs) gave the most robust reduction (- 3.94 bpm, - 5.11 ~ - 2.77). In pairwise meta-analysis, CoQ10 lowered NT-proBNP and improved NYHA status (risk ratio [RR] for ≥ 1-class improvement 1.23, 1.10 ~ 1.38). Network inconsistency was significant for LVESD (P = 0.008). Certainty of evidence (GRADE) was low to very low, and moderate only for n-3 PUFAs; all supplements were well tolerated.
CONCLUSIONS: In this network, higher-dose CoQ10 (150 mg/d) showed the most favourable overall profile for systolic function and ventricular dimensions, while n-3 PUFAs offered the most reliable benefit for heart rate. Given small samples, predominantly Chinese open-label trials, a heterogeneous and time-varying CT comparator, local inconsistency, and poor safety reporting, these findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger, well-designed international RCTs with longer follow-up.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Systematic Review; Network Meta-Analysis

Title: Effect of vitamin D supplementation on serum vitamin D levels and health outcomes in pediatric population with obesity/overweight: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Because 25-hydroxy cholecalciferol is lipophilic, children with obesity/overweight are at increased risk of its deficiency, potentially leading to health issues such as compromising bone mineralization and cardiometabolic health.
OBJECTIVES: Our goal was to assess the impact of 25-hydroxy cholecalciferol supplementation on serum Vitamin D levels and various health parameters such as BMI and cardiovascular risk markers.
METHODOLOGY: Data were extracted from PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar. Following search string was used in each database: (Vitamin D OR 25(OH)D OR cholecalciferol) AND (Obese OR Overweight) AND (randomized trial OR RCT OR intervention) AND (children OR adolescent OR pediatric). Clinical trials assessing the impact of 25-hydroxy cholecalciferol D supplementation in pediatric populations with overweight or obesity, regardless of formulation, dosage, or duration, were included. A total of 24 studies were included in the systematic review, of which 11 randomized controlled trials were eligible for meta-analysis. The included studies' quality was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias (ROB-2) tool. Primary outcome was serum Vitamin D levels while secondary outcomes include cardiovascular risk markers, lipid profile, insulin sensitivity, and change in BMI. Follow-up done at 8 weeks, 12 weeks, 24 weeks, 26 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, and 12 months.
RESULTS: Supplementing with 25-hydroxy cholecalciferol significantly raised the levels of serum vitamin D in children with obesity/overweight. No adverse events occurred following supplementation. Decrease in BMI, serum triglycerides and inflammatory markers were observed but its effects on metabolism and cardiovascular health remained insignificant. According to meta-analysis, vitamin D supplementation (interventional) arm group differed from the placebo by a standardized mean difference of 3.12 ng/ml (95% CI:1.72-4.52).
CONCLUSION: Vitamin D supplementation in children with overweight /obesity correct the deficiency and significantly raise Vitamin D levels with no adverse events. To assess effective therapies to enhance metabolic and cardiovascular outcomes in the pediatric population with overweight/obesity, new trials should be conducted.

Title: Comparative Cardiorenal Efficacy and Safety of SGLT2 Inhibitors and Finerenone in Chronic Kidney Disease With Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
Abstract:
AIMS: No randomized trial has compared SGLT2 inhibitors with finerenone in chronic kidney disease (CKD) with Type 2 diabetes. We estimated their comparative cardiorenal efficacy and safety.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL and trial registries were searched from inception to August 2026 for placebo-controlled outcome trials. Hazard ratios (HRs) were pooled in a frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis, and the between-class contrast was derived indirectly through placebo. Risk of bias followed RoB 2 and certainty followed CINeMA.
RESULTS: Ten trial datasets formed a star network without closed loops. Versus placebo, both classes reduced kidney function progression (SGLT2 inhibitors HR: 0.64, 95% CI: 0.56-0.73; finerenone 0.84, 0.77-0.92) and heart-failure hospitalization (0.61, 0.53-0.69; 0.78, 0.66-0.92). Indirectly, SGLT2 inhibitors were favoured for kidney function progression (0.76, 0.64-0.90) and heart-failure hospitalization (0.77, 0.63-0.95), with no significant difference for atherothrombotic events or mortality. The kidney contrast remained significant after excluding high-risk-of-bias datasets, restricting to dedicated CKD trials and applying a uniform endpoint; the heart-failure contrast did not persist in dedicated CKD trials. Finerenone increased hyperkalemia without increasing acute kidney injury. Certainty was low or very low for every between-class comparison.
CONCLUSIONS: SGLT2 inhibitors and finerenone both provide cardiorenal protection and appear complementary rather than interchangeable. Indirect differences favouring SGLT2 inhibitors derive from a loop-free network with unverifiable transitivity and low certainty; they are hypothesis-generating and should not be used to rank the agents. Safety domains are not reported comparably across classes.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: CRD420261439899.

Title: Interpretation and reporting of coronary computed tomographic angiography (2026 update): An expert consensus document of the Society of Cardiovascular Computed Tomography (SCCT).

OCT-guided versus angiography-guided stent optimisation for post-interventional FFR in patients with complex coronary artery lesions: protocol for a multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial (PRECISION-COMPLEX).
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Whether intravascular imaging-guided percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) reduces adverse events in complex coronary lesions remains debated. Although optical coherence tomography (OCT) improves stent optimisation, its effect on the physiological result of PCI has not been tested in a dedicated randomised trial. The PREcise percutaneous coronary intervention for stent OptimizatION in treatment of COMPLEX lesion (PRECISION-COMPLEX) trial aims to determine whether algorithm-driven OCT-guided stent optimisation improves the physiological result of PCI, assessed by post-optimisation fractional flow reserve (FFR), compared with angiography-guided PCI.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: PRECISION-COMPLEX is an investigator-initiated, multicentre, open-label, superiority randomised controlled trial at four Korean academic hospitals. Patients with stable or unstable angina and at least one prespecified complex lesion are randomised 1:1 to OCT-guided or angiography-guided PCI with current-generation drug-eluting stents. In the OCT arm, stent sizing follows a prespecified algorithm, and post-PCI OCT must confirm adequate expansion, apposition and absence of major edge dissection. Post-PCI FFR is mandated in both arms. The primary endpoint is the proportion of patients with a suboptimal post-optimisation FFR (<0.85); secondary endpoints at 2 years include target-vessel failure and its components, any revascularisation and stent thrombosis. A total of 320 patients gives 90% power to detect a reduction in the primary endpoint from 30% to 15%. Enrolment ran from 15 November 2022 to 4 December 2024; follow-up is ongoing, with main results expected in early 2027.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: The trial protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Chonnam National University Hospital (CNUH-2022-283), the Institutional Review Board of Samsung Medical Center (SMC2022-11-012), the Institutional Review Board of Seoul National University Hospital (H2303-104-1414) and the Institutional Review Board of Chung-Ang University Gwangmyeong Hospital (2212–048-077). It conforms to the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice. All participants provide written informed consent. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication and presentation at scientific meetings. PRECISION-COMPLEX will define the incremental impact of OCT-based optimisation on the physiological result of PCI and indicate whether anatomy-integrated and physiology-integrated guidance improves outcomes in complex coronary lesions.
