Title: Conduction System Versus Right Ventricular Pacing in Patients Undergoing TAVR: A Multicenter Propensity-Matched Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pacemaker implantation after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is common and has been associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Cardiac physiological pacing (CPP) may preserve ventricular synchrony and reduce heart failure (HF) events compared with right ventricular pacing (RVP).
OBJECTIVES: This study sought to compare long-term clinical outcomes of CPP vs RVP in patients requiring permanent pacing after TAVR.
METHODS: Registro de Estimulación Fisiológica-TAVR is a retrospective, multicenter nationwide registry including patients undergoing TAVR and pacemaker implantation within 30 days. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed using baseline clinical and echocardiographic variables, yielding 466 matched pairs. The primary endpoint was the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization. Cox proportional hazards models were used for time-to-event analyses. Median follow-up was 24 months.
RESULTS: In the propensity score-matched cohort, CPP was associated with a lower incidence of the primary endpoint than RVP (9.7% vs 17.6%; HR: 0.57; 95% CI: 0.39-0.83; P = 0.003). This difference was driven by fewer HF hospitalizations (7.9% vs 13.9%; HR: 0.57; 95% CI: 0.37-0.86; P = 0.008). No significant differences were observed in cardiovascular death or all-cause mortality between groups.
CONCLUSIONS: In this multicenter propensity score-matched study, CPP after TAVR was associated with a lower risk of the primary endpoint, driven by fewer HF hospitalizations. These findings support the need for further randomized clinical trials to evaluate the role of CPP in post-TAVR patients requiring ventricular pacing.
Publication Types: Comparative Study; Journal Article; Multicenter Study; Observational Study

Title: Impact of Extent of Coronary Artery Disease in Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A PRO-TAVI Substudy.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coronary artery disease is present in one-half of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). The recent randomized controlled PRO-TAVI (Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Before Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation) trial indicated that deferral of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is safe in patients with concomitant coronary artery disease at 1-year follow-up. The SYNTAX (Synergy between Percutaneous Coronary Intervention with TAXUS and Cardiac Surgery) score quantifies the extent of coronary artery disease, which may guide individualized revascularization strategies.
OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between SYNTAX score (SS) and clinical outcomes in patients undergoing TAVR.
METHODS: This study was a substudy of the PRO-TAVI trial, including 466 patients with significant coronary artery disease undergoing TAVR randomized to deferral of PCI or PCI before TAVR. SS was calculated from preprocedural coronary angiograms, and patients were stratified by SS quartiles. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and major bleeding at 1 year. An ischemic composite outcome of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, and stroke was also assessed.
RESULTS: The primary composite outcome did not differ across SS categories between the deferral and PCI groups at 1-year follow-up, which was completed by all but 1 patient. In patients with SS >17, the ischemic composite outcome occurred more often in the deferral group (30.9% vs 14.8%; adjusted HR: 2.43; 95% CI: 1.04-5.64; P = 0.04), driven primarily by all-cause mortality and stroke. Bleeding events were less frequent in the deferral group across all SS subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with concomitant coronary artery disease undergoing TAVR, deferral of PCI reduced bleeding risk and appeared safe across all SS categories. Deferral of PCI in patients with more complex coronary artery disease (SS >17) was associated with higher risk for the ischemic composite outcome. These post hoc findings require confirmation in randomized trials. (Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Before Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation [PRO-TAVI]; NCT05078619).
Publication Types: Journal Article; Randomized Controlled Trial; Multicenter Study

Title: Immediate Versus Staged Complete Revascularization in Multivessel Disease and STEMI: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: For patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and multivessel disease, complete revascularization is recommended. The timing of nonculprit lesion intervention, either immediately during the index procedure or staged at a later time, has been investigated in randomized controlled trials (RCTs).
OBJECTIVES: This study sought to perform a meta-analysis of RCTs comparing immediate vs staged complete revascularization in patients with multivessel disease presenting with STEMI.
METHODS: We conducted a frequentist, pairwise meta-analysis. Studies were selected based on the following inclusion criteria: multicenter RCTs comparing immediate vs staged nonculprit revascularization in patients presenting with STEMI; exclusive use of second-generation (or newer) drug-eluting stents; a follow-up duration of ≥1 year; and publication in a peer-reviewed journal. The primary outcome of interest was all-cause mortality, whereas secondary outcomes included myocardial infarction (MI), cardiac death, and unplanned revascularization. Summary estimates were computed using random-effects models with inverse-variance weighting based on trial-level HRs and 95% CIs. The study protocol was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251124207).
RESULTS: After a systematic search, 4 randomized trials comprising 2,651 patients were included in the meta-analysis. The risk of all-cause death at 1-year was higher with immediate complete revascularization (HR: 1.50; 95% CI: 1.02-2.21; P = 0.04; prediction interval [PI]: 0.80-2.81; I2 = 0%; t2 = 0). Immediate complete revascularization reduced the risk of recurrent MI when using the protocol specified definitions which included procedural MI (HR: 0.58; 95% CI: 0.36-0.94; P = 0.02; PI: 0.22-1.54; I2 = 0%; t2 = 0.034) but did not reduce risk of spontaneous MI (HR: 0.91; 95% CI: 0.55-1.48; P = 0.90; PI: 0.41-2.00; I2 = 0%; τ2 = 0.00). The risk of cardiac death and unplanned revascularization was comparable between the treatment groups.
CONCLUSIONS: In STEMI and multivessel disease, immediate complete revascularization may be associated with an increased risk of all-cause death at 1-year when compared with staged complete revascularization. The treatment effect on mortality should be interpreted cautiously because of the relatively low number of deaths across the 4 trials and the statistical fragility of the findings. The findings from this analysis do not support an immediate complete revascularization strategy in these patients.

Title: Occlusion-Focused Triage vs Very-High-Risk NSTEMI Criteria: A DIFOCCULT-3 Substudy.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The current ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)/NSTEMI framework may not fully identify patients with ACO who present without diagnostic STE. Although immediate invasive management is recommended for patients with very-high-risk NSTEMI features, these criteria are inconsistently applied in clinical practice. The OMI/NOMI framework has been proposed as an alternative strategy.
OBJECTIVES: This study sought to compare the occlusive and nonocclusive myocardial infarction (OMI/NOMI) classification with guideline-defined very-high-risk non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) criteria for the identification of acute coronary occlusion (ACO) in patients without diagnostic STE.
METHODS: This was a substudy of the multicenter, cluster-randomized DIFOCCULT-3 (Time for a Diagnostic Paradigm Shift From ST-Elevation/Non-ST-Elevation to Occlusion/Non-Occlusion Myocardial Infarction-3) trial. Consecutive adult patients without diagnostic STE on the admission electrocardiogram were included and managed according to either the conventional STEMI/NSTEMI or the OMI/NOMI approach. Very-high-risk NSTEMI was defined according to current guidelines. Outcomes included immediate invasive management (within 2 hours) and adjudicated ACO.
RESULTS: Among 4,398 patients, very-high-risk NSTEMI criteria identified a small proportion of patients and were inconsistently translated into early intervention. The OMI/NOMI approach selected more patients for early invasive management compared with the STEMI/NSTEMI framework (45.4% vs 13.6%; P < 0.001). Adjudicated ACO was identified within 2 hours more frequently under the OMI/NOMI approach (35.1% vs 16.7%; P < 0.001), without reduction in angiographic yield.
CONCLUSIONS: An occlusion-focused diagnostic approach was associated with substantially higher rates of immediate invasive management and earlier identification of patients with adjudicated ACO.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Multicenter Study; Comparative Study; Randomized Controlled Trial

Title: Obesity and Change in NT-proBNP with Angiotensin-Neprilysin Inhibition in Patients with Mildly Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction and a Worsening Heart Failure Event: PARAGLIDE-HF.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine the relationship between obesity status and the effect of sacubitril/valsartan (sac/val) vs valsartan (val) on change in NT-proBNP and a hierarchical outcome of clinical benefit among patients with heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF).
BACKGROUND: In the PARAGLIDE-HF trial, patients with HFpEF and a recent worsening HF event randomized to sac/val vs. val had a greater decrease in NT-proBNP over 8 weeks and showed a trend towards clinical benefit. Patients with HFpEF and obesity represent a unique population with high symptom burden and elevated risk for HF hospitalization. The efficacy and safety of sac/val in this high-risk population following a recent worsening HF event is not well characterized.
METHODS: To assess the interaction between obesity status and sac/val vs val on NT-proBNP, the time-averaged proportional change in NT-proBNP from baseline to Weeks 4 and 8 was assessed with an analysis of covariance model that included the interaction of treatment-by-BMI group (obese with BMI ≥30 kg/m2 vs not obese with BMI 18.5 to <30 kg/m2). A win ratio consisting of a hierarchy of cardiovascular death, total HF hospitalizations, urgent HF visits, and change in NT-proBNP was calculated for both BMI groups.
RESULTS: Overall, 65% (n=298) of participants had obesity and 35% (n=164) of participants did not have obesity. When the interaction between BMI category and the effect of sac/val vs val on the time-averaged proportional change from baseline NT-proBNP was assessed, participants with obesity had a numerically larger decrease in NT-proBNP (ratio of change 0.82 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.99) with obesity vs 0.96 (95% CI 0.71 to 1.29) without obesity that was not statistically significant, p interaction 0.37. Participants with obesity were significantly more likely to derive benefit overall from sac/val vs val as compared to participants without obesity (win ratio 1.38, 95% CI 1.01-1.90 vs 0.90, 95% CI 0.62-1.32, p-interaction = 0.09).
CONCLUSION: In this prespecified secondary analysis of PARAGLIDE-HF, patients with HFpEF and obesity had a similar magnitude of decrease in NT-proBNP with randomization to sac/val vs val, but may derive greater clinical benefit as assessed by a win ratio. This hypothesis-generating evidence suggests that patients that patients with obesity and HFpEF may particularly benefit from sac/val.

Title: Effectiveness and safety of target-specific RNA-based lipid-lowering therapies: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
Abstract: RNA-based therapies target distinct pathways involved in lipid metabolism and may therefore exhibit differential pharmacological effects according to their molecular targets. However, comparative evidence regarding the effectiveness and safety of these target-specific therapies remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of PCSK9-, APOC3-, and ANGPTL3-targeting RNA-based therapies in patients with hyperlipidemia or hypertriglyceridemia. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing inclisiran, olezarsen, plozasiran, or zodasiran with placebo. Treatment effects were expressed as mean differences (MDs) or risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and pooled analyses were stratified according to molecular target. Sixteen randomized controlled trials involving 5604 participants were included. PCSK9-targeting therapy produced the greatest reductions in LDL-C (MD -53.01%, 95% CI -57.56 to -48.45), ApoB (MD -39.59%, 95% CI -43.33 to -35.85), and non-HDL-C (MD -44.62%, 95% CI -47.73 to -41.51), whereas APOC3-targeting therapies produced the greatest reduction in triglycerides (MD -52.26%, 95% CI -56.50 to -48.02). Total adverse events, serious adverse events, and adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were comparable between RNA-based therapies and placebo. Overall, these findings indicate that RNA-based lipid-lowering therapies exhibit target-specific pharmacological effects, with PCSK9 inhibition predominantly reducing atherogenic lipoproteins and APOC3 inhibition producing greater triglyceride lowering. Although the overall safety profile was comparable with placebo, differences in individual adverse outcomes and the limited availability of long-term clinical outcome data highlight the need for further investigation.

Title: Edible fungus polysaccharides and metabolism: A review.
Abstract: Metabolic disorders constitute a severe global health challenge, with dietary intervention serving as a cornerstone of prevention and treatment. As primary bioactive macromolecules isolated from edible fungus, Edible Fungus Polysaccharides (EFPs) possess a broad spectrum of physiological activities. This review consolidates recent progress surrounding EFPs, encompassing extraction techniques, structural features, gut microbiota-driven biotransformation within the body, and how these compounds help sustain metabolic homeostasis. EFPs tune glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism through crosstalking signaling cascades, while systemic benefits arise from immunoregulation, anti-inflammatory properties, and signaling communication along the microbiota-gut-brain axis. EFPs have shown promising effects in the treatment of metabolic syndrome, obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and metabolism-associated malignancies. Existing evidence varies considerably by disease setting. While certain data support the use of EFPs as auxiliary reagents in tumor treatment, solid clinical evidence targeting metabolic complications remains largely lacking. Most relevant observations stem from cell cultures and animal experiments. Available clinical datasets focusing on metabolic outcomes tend to be small, short-duration and geographically limited, restricting broader extrapolation. EFPs hold great research potential as preclinical agents to support metabolic wellness, yet efforts to translate these findings into treatments for metabolic disease remain preliminary. Progress toward practical clinical use hinges on conclusive data from large randomized controlled trials, prolonged toxicology evaluation, and comprehensive pharmacokinetic characterization. Such work will lay the groundwork to define consistent safety benchmarks, therapeutic efficacy and suitable dosage protocols.

Title: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis comparing Myval versus Sapien 3 transcatheter heart valves in severe aortic stenosis: focus on early and one-year mortality.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is a guideline-recommended treatment for severe aortic stenosis (AS). While the balloon-expandable Edwards Sapien 3 valve has long been the benchmark, the newer Myval valve has emerged as a potential alternative. Comparative data on mid-term survival, specifically one-year all-cause mortality, are lacking but crucial for clinical evaluation.
METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesised direct comparative evidence on the Myval versus Sapien 3 valves in patients undergoing TAVI, searching PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central up to November 2025. The primary outcomes included all-cause mortality within 30 days and 1 year. Secondary outcomes were 30-day safety events and hemodynamic parameters.
RESULTS: Five studies (n = 2771) were included. The pooled analysis indicated no statistical difference in 30-day mortality (RR: 1.05, 95% CI: 0.53-2.07; p = 0.89; I2=0%) or in one-year all-cause mortality (RR: 0.93, 95% CI: 0.64-1.35; p = 0.70; I2=0%). Rates of stroke, major bleeding, pacemaker implantation, and other 30-day complications were also comparable (all p > 0.05). Hemodynamically, the Myval valve was superior at 30 days, with a lower mean gradient (MD: -2.37, 95% CI: -3.45 to -1.30; p < 0.0001) and larger effective orifice area (MD: 0.26, 95% CI: 0.17-0.35; p < 0.00001). Available one-year data from two randomised trials indicated this hemodynamic benefit was sustained.
CONCLUSION: This updated meta-analysis demonstrates that the newer Myval valve offers comparable early safety and one-year survival to the established Sapien 3 valve, with superior and sustained hemodynamic performance. These findings support its role as a safe and effective alternative in the TAVI landscape.

Title: Beyond the Average Patient: The Ergodicity Problem in Evidence-Based Medicine and a Proposal for Individual-Dynamic Medicine.
Journal: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
Abstract:
RATIONALE: Evidence-based medicine (EBM) replaced authority with appraisal and has reduced harm. Its own methodologists have documented a persistent gap between what its methods conclude and what its practice does: average effects that are marginal for most treated patients, guidelines that misfit the individual, widespread difficulty converting relative into absolute effects, and no built-in trigger for stopping a treatment that is not helping.
AIMS AND OBJECTIVES: To identify a common source of these problems in the application of population-level estimates to individuals, and to propose a framework that corrects it without abandoning controlled evidence.
METHODS: Conceptual and critical analysis drawing on the methodological critique of EBM published by its founders and leading epidemiologists; the theory of ergodicity in dynamical systems and its empirical tests; the reference class problem; and existing clinical existence proofs of individual-level measurement and closed-loop intervention.
RESULTS: The assumption that a population estimate applies to an individual is the ergodic assumption, which holds when a process is homogeneous across persons and stationary over time. Homogeneity fails whenever treatment response differs between people, which is common; where an individual's responses are reproducible, individual-level inference is both necessary and feasible. Large within-person variability weakens every inference and must be measured rather than assumed away. The N-of-1 randomised trial, which estimates an effect in the individual, was published by Guyatt and Sackett in 1986 and ranks at Level 1 of the Oxford 2011 Levels of Evidence, yet a systematic review found 108 published trials in twenty-five years.
CONCLUSIONS: I propose Individual-Dynamic Medicine, a biocybernetic framework of six principles, each with an existence proof in mainstream medicine, specifying how population evidence and within-person trials divide the work of an individual decision, and state its assumptions, limitations, and the predictions on which it could fail.

Title: Left Atrial Appendage Closure or Medical Therapy in Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The use of anticoagulation in patients with atrial fibrillation is often limited by the significant risk of bleeding, and difficulties maintaining consistent adherence over time. These challenges have led to the development of left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) as an alternative stroke prevention strategy in this patient population. Our study aimed to evaluate LAAC versus medical therapy in patients with atrial fibrillation.
METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted using PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library from database inception through April 1, 2026. The predefined endpoints were composite outcome of systemic embolism, cardiovascular mortality, or stroke in addition to other endpoints including all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, strokes, and major bleeding. All outcomes were pooled using a random effect Mantel-Haenszel model. The between-study variance (τ2) was estimated using the Paul Mendel method, which is the preferred method when the number of included studies is small.
RESULTS: A total of five randomized controlled trials, 5,404 patients were analyzed; 2,878 underwent LAAC and 2,526 received medical therapy. The median follow-up across studies was 4 years. LAAC met noninferiority compared with medical therapy in atrial fibrillation for major bleeding (RR 0.86; 95% CI 0.59-1.26) and all-cause mortality (RR 0.93; 95% CI 0.71-1.22). In contrast, noninferiority was not met for the composite outcome (RR 0.97; 95% CI 0.64-1.47), cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.86; 95% CI 0.51-1.42), systemic embolism (RR 1.93; 95% CI 0.21-17.5), and all stroke (RR 1.11; 95% CI 0.73-1.67).
CONCLUSION: This meta-analysis showed that LAAC was noninferior to anticoagulation for all-cause mortality and major bleeding, but it did not meet noninferiority for the other assessed outcomes, including stroke, cardiovascular mortality, and/or systemic embolism.

Title: Comparison of Effectiveness of Caudal Dexmedetomidine vs. Caudal Fentanyl with Bupivacaine during Pediatric Cardiac Surgery with regards to Hemodynamic Fluctuations and Postoperative Pain.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Optimum analgesia, reflecting into attenuation of stress response, is pertinent in pediatric cardiac surgery. Narcotics are still the mainstay in providing analgesia, and they are a common adjunct in caudal epidural analgesia. Unwanted effects of narcotics warrant a constant search for nonopioid analgesics.
OBJECTIVE: To compare dexmedetomidine vs. fentanyl as an adjuvant in caudal anesthesia in pediatric cardiac surgery.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Sixty patients, 1 to 8 years of age, with acyanotic congenital heart disease were divided into two groups randomly: group A received caudal dexmedetomidine 0.5 µg/kg with 2 mg/kg bupivacaine diluted to 1.6 ml/kg with normal saline. Group B received caudal fentanyl 1 µg/kg with 2 mg/kg bupivacaine diluted to 1.6 ml/kg with normal saline.
RESULTS: Stress response assessed by surge in heart rate and blood pressure after induction was significantly lower in group A (Dexmedetomidine group). The mean time to successful discontinuation of mechanical ventilation was significantly lower in the dexmedetomidine group (1.2 ± 0.4 vs. 1.73 ± 0.58 h). Children in the dexmedetomidine group had lower FLACC pain scores at 4 hours postextubation (2.93 ± 1.04 vs. 3.83 ± 0.83), implying better pain control. The time to need for rescue analgesia was longer in the dexmedetomidine group (6.1 ± 1.21 vs. 3.96 ± 0.96 h).
CONCLUSION: Caudal dexmedetomidine gave better control of hemodynamic parameters when compared with fentanyl and was associated with earlier extubation postoperatively. It also has superior and prolonged analgesia compared to caudal fentanyl as an adjunct.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Comparative Study; Randomized Controlled Trial

Title: Comparative Efficacy of Pecto-Intercostal Facial Plane Block vs Transversus Thoracic Facial Plane Block Combined with Rectus Sheath Block for Post-Sternotomy Analgesia: A Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ultrasound-guided facial plane blocks are central to enhanced recovery after cardiac surgery (ERACS) protocols, yet evidence comparing pecto-intercostal facial plane block (PIFB) and transversus thoracic facial plane block (TTPB) with rectus sheath block (RSB) remains limited.
METHODS: This prospective, randomized, controlled trial enrolled 100 adult patients (ASA II-III) undergoing elective median sternotomy at a tertiary care hospital in South India. Patients received standardized general anesthesia and were randomized to bilateral PIFB or TTPB (20 mL 0.25% bupivacaine + 4 mg dexamethasone per side) with RSB after cardiopulmonary bypass. The primary outcome was 24-hour postoperative fentanyl consumption. Secondary outcomes included visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores at 0, 3-, 6-, 12-, and 24-hours post-extubation, rescue analgesia, extubation timing, ICU/hospital stay, and complications.
RESULTS: A total of 96 patients completed analysis (PIFB: n = 47; TTPB: n = 49). Mean 24-hour fentanyl consumption was 267.23 ± 92.54 µg (PIFB) vs 297.18 ± 88.09 µg (TTPB), mean difference - 29.95 µg (95% confidence interval: -66.60 to 6.70; P = 0.108). VAS scores showed no significant between-group differences (P > 0.05). Rescue analgesia rates were similar, with 84% and 90% not requiring additional opioids. Four PIFB patients (8%) stayed intubated >24 hours due to cardiac issues, vs none in the TTPB group (P = 0.121).
CONCLUSION: This trial found no significant difference in opioid consumption or pain scores between PIFB + RSB and TTPB + RSB for post-sternotomy analgesia. Both techniques were safe within ERACS protocols. Larger noninferiority trials are needed before establishing equivalence or recommending one technique over another.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Randomized Controlled Trial; Comparative Study

Title: The Effect of Intranasal Dexmedetomidine on Hemodynamic Responses during Double-Lumen Tube Insertion: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thoracic surgeries require controlled lung collapse for optimal visualization, achieved through Double-Lumen Tube (DLT) intubation for one-lung ventilation (OLV). DLT insertion triggers significant sympathetic activation, potentially causing cardiovascular complications and cerebrovascular events. This study aimed to investigate the efficacy of intranasally administered Dexmedetomidine in attenuating hemodynamic perturbations associated with laryngoscopy and DLT placement.
METHODS: This randomized controlled study was done in a tertiary care center in South India. Patients coming for thoracic surgery requiring DLT insertion were recruited and randomized into Group A and Group B (n = 25). Group A received 1 mcg/kg Intranasal Dexmedetomidine, and Group B received Intranasal Normal saline 45 minutes prior to induction of anaesthesia using a mucosal atomizer device. Hemodynamic parameters, including systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), and heart rate (HR), were recorded at different time points up to 30 minutes after intubation.
RESULTS: Patients in the dexmedetomidine group had a lower heart rate before intubation (84.92 ± 0.0349) than those in the placebo group (96.48 ± 0.0349). A statistically significant reduction in heart rate was observed in Group A at intubation (T0) and at subsequent time points (T1, T2, T3, T20, T25, and T30). SBP and DBP decreased before intubation, after which subsequent readings showed a statistically significant difference (P = 0.000). Patients in Group A required significantly less Propofol to maintain BP within 20% of baseline.
CONCLUSION: Administering a single dose of intranasal dexmedetomidine at 1 mcg/kg before induction effectively manages the hemodynamic response during laryngoscopy.

Title: Bivalirudin Versus Heparin and Protamine in Adult Patients Undergoing Cardiac Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To summarize the evidence on the morbidity, mortality, and transfusion requirements of adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery using bivalirudin for anticoagulation compared to unfractionated heparin (UFH).
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: A total of 407 patients in three randomized controlled trial (RCTs) were included for pooled analysis. There was no significant difference in the primary outcome; reexploration for hemorrhage between groups (risk ratio: 1.38, 95% confidence interval: 0.42 to 4.48). There were no observable differences in any of the secondary outcomes; thromboembolic events (myocardial infarction, stroke, pulmonary embolism), mortality, or postoperative transfusion requirements (packed red cells (PRC), platelets, cryoprecipitate, fresh frozen plasma (FFP)). All studies included were assessed to have some concern for risk of bias. Interstudy heterogeneity was low across all comparisons.
CONCLUSION: Bivalirudin has not been shown to have any significant difference to UFH on clinical outcomes in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, and as per current international guidelines, can be considered for safe use in those patients for whom UFH is contraindicated. The study is limited by the bias of the included studies and the variability of bivalirudin drug dosage and its therapeutic monitoring; further, well-powered RCTs are required.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Systematic Review; Meta-Analysis; Comparative Study

Title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Insulin Versus Insulin for Perioperative Glycemic Control in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Undergoing Cardiac Surgery: A Systematic Review.
Abstract: Perioperative hyperglycemia is common in patients with type 2 diabetes undergoing cardiac surgery and is linked to adverse outcomes. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) offer glucose-dependent insulinotropic effects and potential cardiac benefits, but their perioperative role remains uncertain. This review evaluated the efficacy and safety of GLP-1 RA therapy as an adjunct to insulin in this setting. Three electronic databases (PubMed, Cochrane, and Google Scholar) were searched for relevant articles up to October 2025. The primary endpoint was blood glucose levels during the perioperative period, while secondary endpoints included hypoglycemia incidence, total insulin requirement, time in target glucose range, and postoperative complications. Three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) including 168 patients with type 2 diabetes undergoing cardiac surgery were assessed. Perioperative use of liraglutide (subcutaneously in doses of 0.6-1.8 mg/day) was associated with preliminary evidence of improved glycemic control across preoperative, intraoperative, and early postoperative periods, including lower glucose levels, reduced glycemic variability, and fewer insulin adjustments, with a low incidence of hypoglycemia. However, heterogeneity in dosing, timing, and monitoring protocols across studies limits direct comparisons. Mild gastrointestinal adverse events, such as nausea and vomiting, were more frequent with liraglutide. One study reported exploratory immunometabolic effects in adipose tissue. Preliminary evidence from these heterogeneous studies suggests that adding liraglutide to insulin may improve perioperative glycemic control compared to insulin or placebo in patients with type 2 diabetes undergoing cardiac surgery. However, findings are limited by the small number of studies, methodological variability, and lack of long-term outcomes, necessitating larger, standardized trials.

Title: Correction to: Sacubitril/valsartan compared to equivalent/sub-equivalent dose angiotensin receptor blocker or angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: a meta-analysis of randomized trials.

Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Society of Cardiovascular Surgery/Canadian Association of Interventional Cardiology Clinical Practice Update on Transcatheter Mitral and Tricuspid Valve Intervention: Patient Evaluation and Management.
Abstract: The management of mitral valve (MV) and tricuspid valve (TV) regurgitation has undergone significant transformation during the past decade. This change has been driven by a growing understanding of the adverse clinical consequences of these conditions, particularly their strong association with heart failure progression, reduced quality of life, and increased mortality-and by the emergence of effective transcatheter options for valve intervention. Among these, transcatheter MV edge-to-edge repair and replacement and transcatheter tricuspid edge-to-edge repair and replacement have become important therapeutic tools that provide a less invasive alternative to surgery in appropriately selected patients. In this clinical practice update we aim to provide contemporary, evidence-based guidance for clinicians in the evaluation and management of patients with severe, symptomatic MV or TV regurgitation who might benefit from transcatheter intervention. Key topics include the clinical presentation of these valve lesions, the diagnostic evaluation with emphasis on multimodality imaging and hemodynamics, criteria for patient selection, and current data on procedural and long-term clinical outcomes. A central theme is the role of timely referral and structured assessment to avoid missed opportunities for intervention. Optimal outcomes require active engagement from referring physicians and close collaboration within a multidisciplinary heart team, including cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, imaging specialists, heart failure specialists, and nursing partners-to ensure careful patient selection, procedural planning, and comprehensive post-intervention follow-up. By integrating clinical judgement with guideline-based recommendations and procedural expertise, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair or transcatheter valve replacement can offer substantial symptomatic relief and improved quality of life for selected patients, while minimizing procedural risk and enhancing overall cardiovascular outcomes.

Title: The Impact of Statin Therapy on Postoperative Short- and Long-term Mortality and Morbidity After Non-Cardiac Surgery.
Abstract:
AIMS: Statins' anti-inflammatory and endothelial-stabilising effects suggest perioperative value, but trials of de novo initiation were discredited following research misconduct. Whether established preoperative statin therapy lowers postoperative mortality dose-dependently remains unclear.
METHODS: We studied 56,362 patients aged ≥45 years undergoing non-cardiac surgery at two university hospitals (2016-2023). Preoperative statin exposure was assessed as status (any vs none), intensity (high vs low/intermediate), and regimen (high vs low/intermediate vs none). Primary outcomes were 30- and 365-day mortality. Inverse probability of treatment weighting, using random forest-estimated propensity scores targeting the average treatment effect in the treated, was applied to balance measured confounders. Associations were estimated with weighted Cox regression.
RESULTS: Overall, 372 patients (0.6%) died within 30 days and 3,735 (6.6%) within 365 days. After weighting, all covariates were balanced. Statin therapy showed a directionally consistent but non-significant association with lower 30-day mortality (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.57-1.07), and was associated with lower 365-day mortality (HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.73-0.90; ARD -1.2 percentage points; number needed to treat 83). A dose-response relationship was evident: versus no statin, high-intensity therapy showed a 29% lower hazard (HR 0.71; 95% CI 0.60-0.83; ARD -2.3 points) and low/intermediate-intensity a 16% lower hazard (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.74-0.96). Findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses.
CONCLUSIONS: Among adults undergoing non-cardiac surgery, established preoperative statin therapy was associated with dose-dependent lower 365-day mortality. These findings suggest perioperative statin continuation as a preventive strategy and warrant confirmation in a randomised trial.

Title: Anticoagulation after transcatheter and surgical bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement: A narrative review.
Abstract: BackgroundBioprosthetic aortic valve replacement, specifically surgical (SAVR) and transcatheter (TAVR), is among the most frequently performed cardiac interventions globally, yet anticoagulation strategies after implantation remain incompletely defined. Atrial fibrillation, notably prevalent pre- and post-operatively in these patients, substantially amplifies thromboembolic risk and complicates decision-making in an already elderly, frail, and comorbid population.ObjectivesTo critically evaluate current anticoagulation strategies after bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement across sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation in both SAVR and TAVR, and to identify evidence gaps and guideline inconsistencies.MethodsWe conducted a narrative review of major international guidelines (ESC/EACTS 2025, ACC/AHA 2020, and NICE 2021) and key clinical trials on antithrombotic therapy in valve replacement populations. Focus was placed on bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement, with mechanical and non-aortic valves excluded.ResultsAspirin monotherapy is the most consistently supported strategy after bioprosthetic TAVR in sinus rhythm, though guidelines diverge on duration and recommendation strength. In atrial fibrillation, all three guidelines apply uniform CHA2DS2-VASc-based frameworks irrespective of AF phenotype, procedural context, or detection modality, reflecting lacking evidence rather than deliberate clinical judgement. No trial has enrolled patients specifically with new-onset post-procedural AF or stratified by AF subtype, and subclinical AF after bioprosthetic AVR remains entirely uncharacterised.ConclusionsGuideline divergence reflects a structurally inadequate evidence base rather than genuine clinical equipoise. Individualised decisions informed by procedure type, AF phenotype, frailty, and bleeding risk are required to guide clinical practice, alongside an adequately powered stratified randomised trial incorporating mandatory continuous rhythm monitoring.

Title: Peptides in urology and sexual medicine: clinical effectiveness, dosing, indications, and safety: a narrative review.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Peptide-based therapies are increasingly used in urology and sexual medicine, although adoption is often influenced by off-label prescribing, direct-to-consumer promotion, and limited long-term safety data. We review mechanisms, clinical evidence, dosing, safety, and regulatory status of these agents.
METHODS: A structured search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar identified studies of peptide-based therapies in sexual medicine. Search terms included Bremelanotide, Melanotan II, Kisspeptin, Oxytocin, PnPP-19, Gonadorelin and growth hormone secretagogues, including GHRP-2, GHRP-6, Ibutamoren, Ipamorelin, Tesamorelin, Sermorelin, and CJC-1295. Of 725 records, 76 studies met inclusion criteria. Findings were synthesized narratively given heterogeneity across studies.
RESULTS: Peptides reviewed act through diverse mechanisms, including central modulation of desire and arousal, stimulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal and growth hormone axes, and nitric oxide-mediated effects on erectile physiology. Bremelanotide and Tesamorelin are the most clinically established agents, with defined dosing and regulatory approval for selected indications. Kisspeptin shows early promise but remains investigational. Growth hormone secretagogues reliably increase growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 concentrations; however, evidence for improved sexual function, physical performance, or quality of life remains limited. Melanotan II, Ibutamoren, CJC-1295, and related agents remain accessible through unregulated markets, raising concerns about product quality, dosing variability, and incompletely characterized adverse effects. Oxytocin has biologic plausibility but limited efficacy data, whereas PnPP-19 remains preclinical. Gonadorelin was Food and Drug Administration approved but is no longer manufactured. Across peptide classes, safety data are limited by short follow-up, small samples, and incomplete assessment of cardiovascular, metabolic, and oncologic outcomes.
DISCUSSION: Peptide-based therapies in urology and sexual medicine show selective therapeutic potential, but most remain insufficiently validated for clinical use. Clinicians should distinguish approved therapies from investigational and nonregulated compounds and counsel patients regarding uncertain benefit, potential harm, and risks of unsupervised use. Randomized trials with standardized dosing and long-term safety assessment are needed before broader adoption.

Title: Rethinking Obstructive Sleep Apnea Care in Obesity: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure, Incretin-Based Therapy, or Both?
Journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity
Abstract: Obesity is a primary driver of obstructive sleep apnea and contributes substantially to its associated cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Although continuous positive airway pressure remains the standard treatment, its efficacy is often limited by suboptimal patient adherence and its impact on cardiovascular outcomes has yet to be consistently established in major clinical trials. Treatments aimed at the underlying problem, excess adiposity, are therefore needed. Weight loss, whether achieved through lifestyle interventions or bariatric surgery is well-known to improve obstructive sleep apnea. The recent introduction of highly effective weight loss medications, most notably incretin-based agents, now offers a pharmacological approach to accomplish the same result. Recent randomized controlled trials in patients with obesity demonstrated that these medications significantly decrease the apnea-hypopnea index and enhance oxygen saturation, with a significant proportion of disease remission. In light of these findings, we propose a therapeutic algorithm stratifying treatment according to symptoms and body mass index. For asymptomatic patients with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea, we suggest incretin-based therapy as a first-line option to concurrently address excessive weight and obstructive sleep apnea. Conversely, in individuals with impaired sleep-related quality of life combining continuous positive airway pressure and incretin therapy may be more appropriate, pairing immediate symptom control with longer-term weight loss. This integrated strategy, prioritizing weight management alongside symptom relief, may offer a comprehensive approach to treat obesity-related obstructive sleep apnea and decrease its associated cardiovascular risks.

Title: Blood pressure and homocysteine-lowering effects of the amlodipine/folic acid combination in patients with hypertension and serum homocysteine concentration ≥10 μmol/l (H-type hypertension): a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, parallel-controlled clinical trial.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elevated plasma homocysteine (Hcy ≥10 μmol/l) and hypertension, defined as H-type hypertension, can synergistically increase the risk of cardiovascular diseases, especially for stroke. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of amlodipine-folic acid in lowering both blood pressure (BP) and plasma Hcy, compared with amlodipine alone.
METHODS: Eligible participants (299 males and 241 females) were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to 5 mg amlodipine (control, group A), 5 mg amlodipine plus 0.4 mg folic acid (group B), or 5 mg amlodipine plus 0.8 mg folic acid (group C). All participants were followed at 2, 4, 6, and 8 weeks. The primary outcome was the efficacy of lowering both BP and Hcy.
RESULTS: Among the 540 participants who were randomized, the efficacy of lowering both BP and Hcy was significantly better in groups B and C compared with group A at the end of 4 weeks, and sustained at the end of 8 weeks (group B vs. group A: 31.7% vs. 6.1%, P < 0.001; group C vs. group A: 32.8% vs. 6.1%, P < 0.001). Both groups B and C were more efficacious in lowering Hcy and raising folate levels than amlodipine alone at 8 weeks. There was no significant difference in BP lowering and adverse events among the three treatment groups.
CONCLUSIONS: In H-type hypertension patients, amlodipine-folic acid (5 mg/0.4 mg or 5 mg/0.8 mg) had a significantly higher efficacy of lowering both BP and plasma Hcy compared with amlodipine alone. The efficacy of BP lowering and safety profile were comparable among the three treatment groups. This trial was registered in clinicaltrials.gov, identifier: NCT01848873.

Title: Oral Anticoagulant Monotherapy vs. Combination Therapy in Chronic Coronary Syndrome Requiring Long-Term Anticoagulation: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
Journal: Clinical and applied thrombosis/hemostasis : official journal of the International Academy of Clinical and Applied Thrombosis/Hemostasis
Abstract: IntroductionEvidence surrounding the optimal antithrombotic regimen for patients with chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) requiring oral anticoagulation remains scarce. This meta-analysis evaluates the efficacy and safety of oral anticoagulant (OAC) monotherapy compared to OAC plus single antiplatelet therapy (SAPT) in this population.MethodsWe systematically searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) till February 2026 comparing OAC monotherapy versus OAC plus SAPT in patients with CCS. Primary outcomes included major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding, net adverse clinical events (NACE), all-cause mortality, and cardiovascular (CV) deaths. Pooled risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated.ResultsOAC monotherapy was associated with a significantly lower risk of major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding compared with dual antithrombotic therapy (DAT) (RR: 0.50; 95% CI: 0.38-0.65; p < 0.001; I2 = 42%). Similarly, OAC monotherapy significantly reduced the incidence of NACE (RR: 0.64; 95% CI: 0.50-0.81; p < 0.001; I2 = 64%). There was no significant difference between the two strategies in all-cause mortality (RR: 0.79; 95% CI: 0.55-1.13; p = 0.20; I2 = 52%). However, OAC monotherapy was associated with a significantly lower risk of CV mortality (RR: 0.71; 95% CI: 0.53-0.97; p = 0.03; I2 = 3%).ConclusionIn patients with CCS requiring long-term oral anticoagulation, OAC monotherapy significantly reduced major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding, CV mortality, and NACE compared with dual antithrombotic therapy (DAT). Rates of major ischemic events, Myocardial Infarction, stroke, and all-cause mortality were comparable between the two strategies.

Title: Effects of adenosine on oxidative stress and inflammation in patients with coronary heart disease underlying percutaneous coronary intervention.
Journal: The Journal of international medical research
Abstract: ObjectiveTo determine whether rapid intracoronary adenosine administration attenuates percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)-induced systemic inflammation and oxidative stress in patients with coronary artery disease.MethodsThis prospective, randomized controlled trial enrolled patients undergoing coronary angiography (coronary angiography group) or PCI. Patients undergoing PCI were assigned to receive intracoronary adenosine (PCI + adenosine group) or placebo (PCI group). Blood levels of inflammatory markers (e.g. cytokines), anti-inflammatory mediators, and oxidative stress indicators (superoxide dismutase and malondialdehyde) were measured before and 24 h after the procedure.ResultsCompared to the coronary angiography group, patients undergoing PCI who received placebo exhibited concurrent elevations in inflammatory and anti-inflammatory markers at 24 h. Intracoronary adenosine significantly suppressed the rise in the levels of inflammatory markers (e.g. interleukin-6 reduced by 35% vs. placebo) and enhanced anti-inflammatory responses (e.g. interleukin-10 increased by 40% vs. placebo). Following PCI, oxidative stress was evident in placebo-treated patients, as reflected by decreased superoxide dismutase activity (15% reduction) and increased malondialdehyde levels (30% elevation). Adenosine restored superoxide dismutase activity to near-baseline levels and reduced malondialdehyde elevation by 85% compared to placebo.ConclusionsIntracoronary adenosine mitigates PCI-associated systemic inflammation and oxidative stress by rebalancing inflammatory pathways and preserving redox homeostasis. These findings highlight its potential as a therapeutic adjunct for improving clinical outcomes following PCI and warrant further validation in large-scale trials.Clinical Trial Registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR); identifier: ChiCTR1800019349.

Title: Prevalence, Health Care Burden, and Longitudinal Outcomes of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Among People With Heart Failure.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Heart failure (HF) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) are common comorbidities. We aimed to assess health care resource use and outcomes associated with COPD in patients hospitalized for HF.
METHODS: This was an exploratory cohort analysis of patients hospitalized for HF and enrolled in the Patient-Centered Care Transitions in HF cluster-randomized trial. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included all-cause and HF hospitalization, health care resource use, and direct health care costs. Survival was evaluated using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for baseline variables.
RESULTS: Among 4441 patients discharged alive, 1136 (25.6%) had COPD at baseline. All-cause mortality was higher at 5 years among patients with vs without COPD (75.2% vs 60.9%, adjusted hazard ratio 1.29, 95% confidence interval 1.19-1.40). Patients with COPD had more frequent all-cause rehospitalizations (mean [standard deviation] 3.4 [6.6] vs 2.7 [8.6] per patient, P = 0.01), but no significant difference in HF rehospitalizations (0.9 [2.3] vs 0.9 [4.5] per patient, P = 0.74). Patients with COPD had more annual physician visits, multidisciplinary clinic visits, and supportive care (all P < 0.01), as well as greater annual direct health care costs in Canadian dollars (at 5 years: $91,888 [$109,319] vs $76,823 [$116,218]) than those without COPD, primarily driven by rehospitalizations.
CONCLUSIONS: Among patients discharged alive after hospitalization for HF, COPD is common and is associated with higher all-cause mortality and all-cause rehospitalizations, greater health care use, and higher direct health care costs. Interventions to reduce the health care burden in HF should include broad approaches that address important comorbidities.

Title: Optical Coherence Tomography Findings Following Intravascular Lithotripsy in Calcified Coronary Artery Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intravascular lithotripsy (IVL) has emerged as a novel technology for modifying calcified coronary lesions, whereas optical coherence tomography (OCT) enables high-resolution assessment of calcium modification and procedural outcomes. However, the mechanistic and procedural effects of IVL assessed by OCT across studies remain incompletely characterized.
METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261332946). PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and Epistemonikos were searched from inception through February 2026. Randomized controlled trials and observational studies with extractable quantitative OCT outcomes were included. The primary endpoint was OCT-detected calcium fracture. Secondary endpoints included multiple calcium fractures, minimum stent area (MSA), stent expansion, acute lumen gain, procedural success, and in-hospital major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs). Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to estimate pooled proportions or mean values with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
RESULTS: Thirty studies encompassing a total of 3030 patients were included. OCT-detected calcium fracture occurred in 68% (95% CI 56%-79%) of lesions, whereas multiple fractures were observed in 34% (95% CI 26%-41%). IVL-treated lesions achieved favorable procedural metrics, including a pooled final MSA of 6.45 (95% CI 6.07-6.82) mm2, stent expansion of 85.9% (95% CI 82.3%-89.5%), and acute lumen gain of 3.50 (95% CI 3.14-3.87) mm2. Procedural success was high (95%, 95% CI 93%-98%) with low in-hospital MACEs (2%, 95% CI 1%-3%). Substantial heterogeneity was observed across endpoints.
CONCLUSIONS: Coronary IVL assessed by OCT is frequently associated with calcium fracture and favorable procedural outcomes with high procedural success and low early adverse events.

Title: Methylphenidate and Long-Term Risk of Cardiovascular Diseases: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: Cardiovascular safety of methylphenidate remains a matter of debate.
METHODS: To evaluate the long-term cardiovascular risk associated with methylphenidate use, a cohort study was conducted using the French National Health Data System. New users were defined by a first methylphenidate dispensation (index date) between January 1, 2014, and December 31, 2023. Each new user was matched with three nonusers by sex and by month and year of birth. Individuals with prior cardiovascular disease or relevant cardiovascular comorbidities were excluded. The primary outcome was cardiovascular disease, defined by International Classification of Diseases codes or antihypertensive drug use. Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HRs), accounting for demographic and clinical covariates. Negative control outcomes were used to assess residual confounding, allowing the derivation of calibrated HRs and confidence intervals.
RESULTS: A total of 212 216 new users and 636 648 matching nonusers were included. Mean age was 13.7 years and 72% were males. Over a follow-up of ~4 years, 3858 cardiovascular diseases occurred (0.45%): 1960 in new users (9.2 per 1000) and 1898 in nonusers (3 per 1000). The adjusted HR was 2.37 (95% CI [2.21; 2.54]), with a calibrated HR of 1.85 (95% CI [1.55; 2.21]).
CONCLUSIONS: The results suggest that methylphenidate use may be associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases. Although the calibrated estimates indicate attenuation due to residual confounding, the association remained statistically significant. This supports recommendations for cardiovascular monitoring during treatment.

Title: Effects of Kinect-based mixed-reality exercise and deep-sea water consumption on metabolic syndrome: a randomized controlled trial.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: The increasing prevalence of metabolic syndrome poses significant health risks, particularly for cardiovascular diseases and type 2 diabetes. Exercise interventions have shown promise in improving the components of metabolic syndrome, including blood pressure, lipid profiles, and glucose metabolism. Kinect-based mixed-reality exercise provides real-time feedback and personalized guidance, making it suitable for unsupervised training. Deep-sea water has beneficial effects on lipid metabolism and insulin sensitivity. However, the effects of Kinect-based mixed-reality exercise and deep-sea water on metabolic syndrome remain unclear.
METHODS: Fifty-six participants aged 30-65 years with a diagnosis of metabolic syndrome were randomly assigned to four groups for an 8-week intervention: control (CG), deep-sea water consumption (WG), Kinect-based mixed-reality exercise (EG), and combined deep-sea water consumption and Kinect-based mixed-reality exercise (WEG). The intervention comprised a 40-min Kinect-based mixed-reality circuit exercise three times per week and daily consumption of 440 mL of deep-sea water. The measurements included blood pressure, body composition, blood profiles, quality of life, physical activity, diet recall, and the metabolic syndrome score.
RESULTS: Forty-eight participants completed the study, demonstrating high compliance with the EG (98.4%) and WG (99.2%). Waist circumference significantly decreased in all intervention groups (WG, p = 0.002; EG, p < 0.0001; WEG, p < 0.0001), with a significant difference between CG and EG (p = 0.020). The metabolic syndrome component score decreased significantly in the EG (p = 0.004) and WEG (p = 0.002) groups, falling below the diagnostic threshold for metabolic syndrome.
CONCLUSION: These findings indicate the potential benefits of combining deep-sea water consumption and Kinect-based mixed-reality exercise in metabolic syndrome management.

Title: Clinical outcomes of sacubitril/valsartan in patients with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction and acute heart failure: a multi-institutional study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The long-term real-world effectiveness and safety of in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan in patients hospitalized for acute heart failure (HF) with mildly reduced or preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (HFmrEF or HFpEF) remain uncertain, particularly among patients with advanced chronic kidney disease or dialysis, who are often underrepresented in randomized trials.
PATIENTS/MATERIALS AND METHODS: We identified 9,107 patients with HFmrEF or HFpEF hospitalized for acute HF from the Chang Gung Research Database between January 1, 2016, and June 30, 2023. Propensity score weighting with overlap weights was applied to balance baseline characteristics between treatment groups. Risks of fatal and nonfatal outcomes were analyzed using Cox proportional hazards and Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models, respectively.
RESULTS: After overlap weighting, the incidence rates of the composite endpoint of HF rehospitalization and cardiovascular (CV) death were 39.7 and 40.3 per 100 person-years in the angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) and angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) groups, respectively (Hazard ratio, 0.97; 95% confidence interval, 0.79-1.20). In analyses stratified by chronic kidney disease stage, the association between treatment group and the primary endpoint was consistent among patients with eGFR ≥60, 30-59, <30 mL/min/1.73 m2, or dialysis.
CONCLUSIONS: In this multi-institutional real-world cohort of patients hospitalized for acute HF with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) >40%, in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan was not associated with lower risks of HF rehospitalization or CV death compared with ARB therapy, despite greater NT-proBNP reduction in a biomarker subcohort. Limited sample size precludes definitive conclusions regarding therapeutic equivalence.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Multicenter Study; Observational Study
